analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse staffing levels for nursing homes that take Medicare or Medicaid, and raises Medicaid payments to help pay for it.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote, leaving no new federal nurse staffing minimums in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nursing homes that receive Medicare or Medicaid money to meet minimum nurse staffing levels set by the Health and Human Services Department, based on a staffing report HHS sent to Congress in March 2002. It would have made facilities post their actual staffing hours publicly, allowed inspectors to review facility finances, and raised federal Medicaid matching payments to states while restoring stricter standards for what Medicaid must pay nursing homes. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents, who would get guaranteed minimum hours of nursing care each day, and their families, who could see staffing data for each facility. Nursing staff would gain from higher demand for their work. States would gain financially because the federal government would permanently pick up an extra 1.5 percentage points of Medicaid costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires every Medicare or Medicaid nursing facility, within two years, to meet minimum staffing levels drawn from the HHS report to Congress of March 21, 2002: at least 2.4 to 2.8 hours of certified nurse aide care per resident per day, 1.15 to 1.3 hours from licensed or registered nurses, and 0.55 to 0.75 of those hours from registered nurses specifically [S2] [S3].
Staff cannot be counted toward the ratios while doing non-nursing work like administration, food preparation, housekeeping, or laundry [S3].

Facilities would have to post a description of the staffing rules and their average hours of nursing care per resident for each of the last four quarters, and keep staffing records that are checked for accuracy during standard surveys [S3].

Standard and extended inspections could include an examination of facility financial records to determine whether Medicare and Medicaid payments are being used consistently with the care requirements [S2] [S3].

To help pay for the staffing, the bill permanently raises the federal Medicaid matching rate for every state by 1.50 percentage points starting in fiscal year 2003, and restores the pre-1997 'Boren amendment' criteria so Medicaid rates must meet reasonable payment standards, with a safe-harbor methodology states can adopt [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, who would bear the cost of hiring more nurses and aides and of opening their financial records to surveyors; and federal taxpayers, who would fund the permanent 1.5-percentage-point increase in the Medicaid match, though that shift lowers what states pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Meeting the HHS ratios would require substantial new hiring of nurses and aides, and the bill itself anticipates that some facilities may not be able to comply within two years, giving the Secretary authority to delay full compliance for up to five years and phase in weaker interim standards instead [S3].
The federal cost is permanent: the 1.5-point increase in every state's federal Medicaid matching percentage applies indefinitely with no expiration or offset [S2] [S3].

Restoring the Boren amendment payment criteria would require states to pay nursing homes at least certain minimum levels, which raises Medicaid costs for state budgets even with the higher federal match [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The staffing and transparency provisions are real protections for a vulnerable population, and the bill partially offsets the cost to facilities by increasing federal Medicaid payments to them through the states. The honest cost is money: more hiring by operators, higher Medicaid rates, and a permanent federal spending commitment. The bill also hedges, letting HHS stretch compliance out over five years if facilities cannot meet the ratios quickly, which softens the guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Nursing Home Staffing Improvement Act of 2002 on May 14, 2002, joined by nine other members including Democratic leader Richard Gephardt and Reps. Dingell, Stark, Brown, Schakowsky, Carson, Norton, Rodriguez, and Markey [S1] [S3] [S5].
Twenty members cosponsored the bill: 19 of the House's 208 Democrats and the chamber's one Independent [S4].

The same day, the Speaker referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, a split referral that means two committees each had to act on the parts in their jurisdiction [S5].

On June 3, 2002, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health. That was its last recorded action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators came out ahead: they avoided the federal staffing minimums, public posting of staffing hours, and financial scrutiny of how Medicare and Medicaid payments are spent. Nursing home residents got none of the new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators, untouched by new mandates

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's single Independent; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding 223 of 432 House seats the bill had no path out of committee without their support.

industries.note: The bill would force operators to hire more nurses and aides to meet federal ratios and open their financial books to inspectors, while also raising Medicaid payment rates through the Boren restoration and sending facilities more federal money via the FMAP increase. The industry's core interest here runs against residents: it benefits from the higher payments but stands to lose from the staffing mandate and audits.

Federal staffing minimums would create demand for tens of thousands of additional direct-care nursing hours, benefiting aides, LPNs, and RNs whose work would also finally be counted only when it is direct care.

States would receive a permanent 1.5-point boost in the federal share of Medicaid costs, lowering state payments, but the reinstated Boren amendment criteria would obligate states to pay providers higher rates.
